title: A quantitative perspective on ethics in large team science
extended_summary:
This paper examines how the growth of large-team science changes the ethical structure of scientific work. The authors ask how trends such as increasing team size, hierarchical organization, bottlenecks in scientific careers, and expanding international collaboration affect core ethical issues in science, including credit assignment, authorship, conflict of interest, mentoring, and the universality of ethical norms.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or an AI tool. Instead, it uses quantitative historical evidence drawn from publication records, patent data, Nobel Prize recipient counts, and U.S. science workforce statistics to illustrate structural changes in science over time. The context is largely the U.S. academic system, with additional cross-national publication collaboration data and comparisons across disciplines such as biology, medicine, physics, and economics.

The authors conclude that science has shifted steadily toward larger, more complex, and more international teams, making traditional institutions designed for singleton or small-team science increasingly inadequate. They argue that these changes weaken transparency and mentor-mentee relationships, complicate fair credit allocation, and increase ethical tensions in authorship and collaboration. The paper ultimately calls for clearer ethical norms, better sanctioning of misconduct, and early cultivation of ethical values in science education.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a conceptual and quantitative commentary on ethics in large-team science, using descriptive historical data rather than an evaluative educational intervention design. It is not an empirical study of AI or science instruction and does not provide the credibility criteria needed for causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct measured impact on K-12 scientific reasoning or inquiry, and it does not evaluate an instructional intervention. Its relevance is indirect and theoretical only, so there is no demonstrable educational effect to rate.

finding.finding_summary: This is a quantitative expository/historical analysis of science-team trends, not a study of K-12 instruction. It documents long-run growth in team size, labor-force bottlenecks, and cross-border collaboration, and argues these shifts create ethical and institutional pressures that science education policy should address. No student learning effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Descriptive trends in publication coauthorship, faculty/postdoc counts, Nobel Prize recipient counts, and international collaboration matrices
